sentences.text: The only known skeleton of Trinisaura belongs to a subadult individual estimated to be 1.5 meters long, though an adult could have reached about 2 meters.
This lightly built, bipedal dinosaur possessed long legs adapted for running and a rigid tail for balance, along with an elongated neck ending in a small, beaked skull adapted for eating plants.
Trinisaura was much smaller than the other named Antarctic ornithopod, Morrosaurus, which was approximately 4 meters long.
Asteraceae pollen grains collected from the formation represent the oldest known records of that plant family.

The fossils of Trinisaura were collected in 2008 by paleontologists Juan Moly and Rodolfo Coria from the Snow Hill Island Formation, and the species Trinisaura santamartaensis was formally described and named in 2013 by Coria, Moly, Reguero, Santillana, and Marenssi.
Based on its phylogenetic position and skeletal remains, Trinisaura was a herbivore.

Histological studies show that Trinisaura exhibited rapid growth with periodic interruptions, similar to other Antarctic ornithopods like Gasparinisaura, yet it also exhibited a slower growth rate than contemporaries in warmer climates, likely an adaptation to the cold Antarctic environment.

The fossils of Trinisaura show minimal transport and reworking, indicating they were deposited in a setting with little disturbance, while wood fragments, twigs, and leaves found in concretions near Trinisaura fossils suggest they arrived via the same ocean currents that transported the dinosaur carcasses in an environment that may have included wet areas similar to peat bogs.
The same formation has yielded fossils of the armored ankylosaur Antarctopelta, a sauropod vertebra, an aquatic elasmosaurid, and carnivorous mosasaurs Taniwhasaurus and Hainosaurus.
Trinisaura is classified as a basal member of the ornithopod clade, and the describers placed it basally within the Euornithopoda group, though it is debated whether it is a basal iguanodontid.

A 2015 discovery found that Trinisaura formed part of the basal iguanodontid group Elasmaria, but a 2022 analysis by Karen Poole found no Elasmaria clade, instead placing Trinisaura in a branch of Rhabdodontoidea with Patagonian and South African genera.
During the Upper Cretaceous, Antarctica had a much warmer climate than today and was covered in forests.
Trinisaura evolved distinct traits due to geographic isolation after Antarctica broke off from the supercontinent Gondwana.

Trinisaura fossils were found on James Ross Island, off the coast of northern Antarctica, and Trinisaura is known only from the Gamma Member of the Snow Hill Island Formation on James Ross Island, located on the northeastern edge of the Antarctic Peninsula.
Trinisaura provides evidence linking ornithopod dinosaurs across the continents that formed the ancient supercontinent Gondwana.
It is debated whether the larger dinosaur Morrosaurus is a junior synonym of Trinisaura, despite several differentiating characteristics.
